subject: Endocarditis

source_quote: Endocarditis usually happens when bacteria or fungus gets into your blood through your mouth or skin and travels to your heart. This could be during a dental procedure or through a cut or graze, for example.

subject: The vegetation is the pathological hallmark of infective endocarditis and
object: the main clinical manifestations. As it grows, it causes continuous bacteraemia with a high bacterial load that can seed distant infections. Invasion of the structures to which it is attached can destroy valves and impair haemodynamics. Pieces of this friable mass can break away and cause distant emboli that can substantially affect function and prognosis.
source: Article: Cuervo G, Escrihuela-Vidal F, Gudiol C et al. Current Challenges in the Management of Infective Endocarditis. Frontiers in Medicine 2021
source_quote: The vegetation represents the pathological hallmark of infective endocarditis and determines its main clinical manifestations, namely: (1) the growth of this “full bacterial lesion” causes continuous bacteremia at a high inoculum that can seed distant septic metastases, (2) the invasion of the structures to which this vegetation is anchored can cause valvular destruction, negatively affecting the patient's hemodynamics, and finally (3) this friable mass can detach pieces that cause distant embolisms, which can significantly affect the function and prognosis of the affected patients.

subject: Transthoracic echocardiography
relation: is the main diagnostic imaging test for
object: endocarditis. Its sensitivity varies for abnormalities of and around the valves, including vegetations (about 65% sensitivity), new regurgitation, prosthetic valve dehiscence, perforations, abscesses and fistulae. Transoesophageal echocardiography detects and characterises local abnormalities better (about 95% sensitivity for intracardiac vegetations), particularly with a negative transthoracic study, valvular or paravalvular complications, prosthetic valve infection or infection associated with cardiac implantable electronic devices.
source: Article: Cuervo G, Escrihuela-Vidal F, Gudiol C et al. Current Challenges in the Management of Infective Endocarditis. Frontiers in Medicine 2021
source_quote: Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) is the main imaging method in the diagnosis of endocarditis, with varying sensitivity rates for valvular and paravalvular abnormalities such as vegetations (sensitivity around 65%), a new regurgitation or dehiscence of a prosthetic valve, perforations, abscesses and fistulae (). Transesophageal echocardiography (TOE) provides a better detection and characterization of local abnormalities (sensitivity for intracardiac vegetations of ~95%), particularly when TTE is negative, in the case of valvular or paravalvular complications as well as in prosthetic valve endocarditis (PVE) and endocarditis associated with CIEDs ().

subject: A variable proportion of endocarditis cases, up to 10–20%,
object: culture-negative endocarditis when no cause is documented. This is most often due to previous antibiotics or infection with fastidious slow-growing microorganisms or truly non-cultivable intracellular bacteria, such as Coxiella burnetii, Chlamydophila species, Bartonella species or Tropheryma whippelii.
source: Article: Cuervo G, Escrihuela-Vidal F, Gudiol C et al. Current Challenges in the Management of Infective Endocarditis. Frontiers in Medicine 2021
source_quote: Finally, a variable proportion (up to 10–20% of cases) without documented etiology are considered “culture-negative endocarditis,” mostly as a consequence of prior administration of antibiotics or caused either by fastidious slow-growing microorganisms or by truly non-cultivable intracellular bacteria (e.g., Coxiella burnetii, Chlamydophila spp, Bartonella spp, Tropheryma whippelii) (,).

subject: People at higher risk of endocarditis

They should clean and cover cuts and grazes properly to avoid infections, wash hands regularly, make sure they and their family, friends or carers know the symptoms, and speak to a doctor before any piercings or tattoos.
source_quote: If you're at higher risk of endocarditis, there are things you can do to lower your chance of getting it. Do take care of your teeth and gums and have regular dental check-ups – you may also be advised to speak to a doctor before having any dental procedures properly clean and cover any cuts and grazes to avoid getting infections wash your hands regularly make sure you and any family, friends or carers know the symptoms of endocarditis Don't do not get any piercings or tattoos without speaking to a doctor first

source_quote: You'll be given antibiotic or antifungal medicine for 4 to 6 weeks to treat the infection. This usually happens in hospital through a drip or injections into your vein (IV) to start with.

subject: During and after recovery from endocarditis, regular check-ups and blood tests
object: make sure the infection has gone and look for damage that could cause other complications such as heart failure.
source_quote: Recovering from endocarditis You will need to have regular check-ups and blood tests during and after your recovery. This is to make sure the infection has gone and to look for any signs of damage that could cause other complications, such as heart failure.

subject: About half of people with endocarditis
object: surgery to remove or repair damaged heart tissue or valves. Depending on the site of infection, a pacemaker may need to be fitted to maintain a normal heartbeat, or an existing pacemaker may need to be removed and replaced.
source_quote: Around half of people who have endocarditis will need surgery to remove or repair damaged heart tissue or valves. Depending on where the infection is, you may also need to have a pacemaker fitted to keep your heart beating normally, or have your pacemaker removed and replaced if you already have one.

subject: If you or someone with you develop possible stroke symptoms,
object: 999 immediately. Signs include facial weakness, with one side possibly drooping and difficulty smiling, weakness or numbness in one arm or one side of the body or inability to raise and hold up both arms, speech problems such as slurring, sounding confused, difficulty speaking or finding words, and blurred vision or loss of sight in one or both eyes. Stroke can complicate endocarditis and needs immediate treatment.
source_quote: Immediate action required: Call 999 if you or someone you're with: has face weakness – one side of the face may droop (fall) and it might be hard to smile has weakness or numbness in one arm or down one side of the body, or cannot fully lift both arms and keep them there has speech problems, such as slurring words, sounding confused, or finding it difficult to speak or find the right words gets blurred vision or loss of sight in one or both eyes These can be signs of a stroke, which can be a complication of endocarditis and needs to be treated immediately.

subject: If you have symptoms of endocarditis, a doctor
object: examine you, listen to your chest and ask about recent dental treatment or other medical procedures. If they suspect endocarditis, you will usually be referred to a heart specialist (cardiologist).
source_quote: If you have symptoms of endocarditis, a doctor will examine you and listen to your chest. They'll ask about any recent dental treatment or other medical procedures you've had. If the doctor thinks you may have endocarditis, you'll usually be referred to a heart specialist (cardiologist).

source_quote: You also have a higher chance of getting endocarditis again, so it's important to know the symptoms and get help quickly if you think you may have it again.
